sentences: This is Johannes Vermeer's The Milkmaid.
A kitchen maid pours milk, slowly and carefully, into an earthenware bowl.
The canvas is less than fifty centimetres on each side, yet before it, time seems to stand still.
Vermeer spent his working life in the Dutch city of Delft, and this painting is thought to date from around 1660.
The Rijksmuseum acquired it in 1908, and it remains one of the finest treasures in the museum's collection.
Light enters from the window on the left.
Passing through the small leaded panes, it fills the room calmly and falls in turn across her yellow bodice, her deep blue apron and the bread on the table.
This soft, steady daylight is one of Vermeer's great signatures.
Her head is bowed, all her attention on the bowl.
Beneath the white cap, her cheek glows in the daylight.
The yellow of her bodice is lead-tin yellow, which shines out with special brightness in this picture.
Watch the thin, steady stream of milk as she pours, never quite breaking.
That white thread is the quiet heart of the picture.
The composition is built on two diagonals that meet right here, by the woman's right wrist.
Vermeer scattered tiny dots of light over the bread crust and the basket so their surfaces seem to glitter, and you can almost feel their roughness.
The blue of the apron is natural ultramarine, a costly pigment ground from lapis lazuli, which he chose over the cheaper azurite.
The same deep blue runs on into the cloth on the table.
On the floor at lower right stands a small foot warmer, and a tile behind it shows Cupid.
Some read them as hints of love or longing; others see simply a practical comfort for someone working in a cool kitchen.
Research by the Rijksmuseum shows he first painted a wall map here and a large clothes basket below, then decided to paint out both.
That leaves her standing like a sculpture against a bare, bright wall, with nothing to distract us.
Now look up at the bare white wall.
Stains, shadows, even a nail and its little nail hole are all kept.
A wall that seems empty is what makes the air of this room feel so real.
Step back and see the whole again.
Vermeer made this picture great not by adding but by taking away.
See how long you can hold your gaze on that brief moment as the milk falls, and how still the room becomes.
